---
internalId: 583d9c88-b71c-4560-92ad-3e23d33bf1d0
---

# Architectural decisions

Project-wide decisions for MDÂ². The app is a Vite React web app in `app/`; `desktop/` is a separate Electron host that can load the website and expose local capabilities through preload bridges.

## File naming

| Decision | Rule | Rationale |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Code files use lowercase snake_case names. | All code files in `app/src/` and `desktop/` use lowercase words separated by underscores, for example `github_auth_service.ts`, `project_workspace.tsx`, and `local_git_service.js`. Test files keep the same base name with `.test` before the extension, for example `github_auth_service.test.ts`. Exported symbols keep normal TypeScript/JavaScript casing such as `GithubAuthService`, `ProjectWorkspace`, and `useGithubAuth`. | A single file naming convention avoids mixed PascalCase, camelCase, and hyphenated filenames, and keeps imports predictable across Windows and case-sensitive environments. |

## Services and state

| Decision | Rule | Rationale |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Global singleton services own domain state and logic. | Each domain is a class in `src/services/**`, instantiated once at module level and exported, for example `export const indexesService = new IndexesService()`. React components do not own domain state. | Keeps business logic out of components, testable without a DOM, and shared across windows/views without Redux, Zustand, or Context stores. |
| Service location follows usage scope. | If a service is specific to one UI element and used only there, place it beside that component. Generic or shared services, such as logging, database access, config, storage, or cross-screen domain logic, belong in `src/services/`. | Keeps component-owned behavior local while preserving `src/services/` for reusable application services. |
| Consumers use direct imports or the service injector. | Direct import when no import cycle exists; use `src/services/service_injector.js` when a cycle would occur. Every global singleton service registers itself in its constructor with `inj.register('myService', this)`. | The service graph is dense; the injector is a bare global registry that defers resolution to call time. |
| Services have a two-phase lifecycle. | Constructors only register and set unloaded state such as `null`. Config-dependent or service-dependent work runs in `init()`, `start()`, app bootstrap (`App.jsx`), or a `loaded` lifecycle event. `configService.config` is private; callers use `get`, `set`, and `clear`. | Module evaluation order is not guaranteed, so `configService` is not usable at import time. Reading config in a constructor is a bug. |

## Card state

| Decision | Rule | Rationale |
| --- | --- | --- |
| The application has one `Card` domain type. | Do not create separate canonical, project, snapshot, or editor card types. The card-owning service holds the loaded cards and exposes focused operations that change only the requested field. React snapshots and editor drafts are read values; they must never replace or merge a complete card. Parser bookkeeping may remain private persistence metadata, but it is not another card model. | One card concept gives state a clear owner and prevents stale copies from overwriting newer worktree, activity, ordering, policy, or body values. |
| Card UI subscribes at field level. | A component subscribes only to the primitive or stable reference it renders, using granular `EventTarget` events and `useSyncExternalStore`. Do not clone or stringify a complete card to detect a field change. Group fields only in a deliberately small, stable projection when they are always rendered together. | A one-field change allocates and rerenders only what consumes that field, keeping memory use bounded and the UI responsive. |
| Cards are serialized only at persistence boundaries. | Mutate the owned `Card` through a focused operation, then serialize its current state when the persistence batch flushes. Editor changes update only the edited field. Activity linking updates only activity references. External file changes are parsed and applied deliberately without replacing dirty local state. | Persistence remains deterministic while concurrent saves and external updates cannot discard unrelated newer values. |


## Events and React integration

| Decision | Rule | Rationale |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Services notify observers through their own `EventTarget`. | Services expose an `EventTarget` and dispatch named `CustomEvent` domain events such as `activeIndex`, `added`, `deleted`, or `changedBox`. Observers subscribe with `addEventListener` and unsubscribe with `removeEventListener` on the owning service. | Decouples producers from consumers without depending on Node `EventEmitter`, which is not available in the browser-first React app. |
| Custom hooks bridge service events to functional components. | Hooks in `src/components/hooks/`, such as `useActiveIndex` and `useProjectConfig`, seed `useState` from a service property, subscribe in `useEffect`, unsubscribe in cleanup, and return the value. Prefer hook + service over prop chains. | Components stay declarative and avoid direct event plumbing. |
| Components subscribe at the smallest rendering boundary. | Root and layout components compose UI regions and pass structural inputs. Components that render changing application data subscribe through hooks themselves. Do not hoist changing data into ancestors only to pass it downward. | Limits rerenders to affected UI, protects transient state such as open popups, and avoids broad prop chains. |
| Components use the app theme service path. | `App` owns theme mode through `useThemeMode()`, builds the MUI theme with `createAppTheme(mode)`, and provides it through `ThemeProvider`. Components read theme values with MUI APIs such as `useTheme`, `useMediaQuery`, and `sx`; only controls that change the palette mode receive `mode` and `onToggleTheme`. | Theme state, persistence, and palette construction stay centralized while components remain presentation-focused. |

internalId: f2ec9e28-8064-4707-bce9-b62f24d57524
---

# App Style Guide â€” Kanban / MDÂ² (React + MUI)

How to build **any new component** so it matches the app. This is written for **Material UI v5+** components.

**The theme is the source of truth.** All color, radius, base typography, and spacing units live in the single `createTheme` (defined in `GUIDANCE.md` Â§1/Â§9). This guide does **not** define colors â€” it tells you **which theme value to use for which role**, and covers the things the theme can't encode: layout, spacing/margins, borders, elevation, and component conventions.

**The one rule that matters:** never write a raw hex, px radius, or magic color into a component. Read it from the theme (`theme.palette.*`, `theme.shape`, `theme.typography`, `theme.spacing`). If a component has a hardcoded hex in its `sx`/styled, it's wrong â€” that's exactly where the look drifts and where dark mode breaks.

---

## 1. How to consume the theme

- **Colors:** `sx={{ color: 'text.secondary', bgcolor: 'background.paper', borderColor: 'divider' }}` â€” MUI resolves dotted palette paths automatically in `sx`. In `styled`/JS use the callback form: `styled(Box)(({ theme }) => ({ color: theme.palette.text.secondary }))`.
- **Spacing:** use the 8px unit via the spacing scale â€” `sx={{ p: 2, gap: 1, mt: 1.5 }}` (`2` = 16px, `1` = 8px). Don't write `padding: '16px'`.
- **Radius:** `borderRadius: 1` (= `theme.shape.borderRadius` = 8) and multiples; for the fixed non-8 radii see Â§4.
- **Typography:** prefer `Typography variant=...` and `theme.typography.*` over ad-hoc `fontSize`.
- **Custom tokens:** roles the default MUI palette doesn't cover (column/track surfaces, the strong/hover border steps, `text-3/4`, section-header color, `primary-bg` tint, status colors) must exist in the theme under a namespace (e.g. `theme.palette.custom.*`) with light + dark values. Consume them the same way â€” `bgcolor: 'custom.column'`. **Never inline their hex.** If a needed token doesn't exist yet, add it to the theme, don't hardcode it in the component.

---

## 2. Role â†’ theme slot

Pick the slot by the element's **role**, not by how it looks in one mode:

| Role | Theme slot |
|---|---|
| App background; tinted footer/action bars | `background.default` |
| Column & sidebar surface | `custom.column` |
| Segmented-control / toolbar track, hover fill | `custom.track` |
| Card, dialog, popup, input surface | `background.paper` |
| Hairlines, resting borders | `divider` |
| Input borders, vertical separators | `custom.borderStrong` |
| Border on hover | `custom.borderHover` |
| Titles, values, headings | `text.primary` |
| Body copy, field labels | `text.secondary` |
| Meta, captions, resting icons | `custom.text3` |
| Muted / placeholder / disabled | `custom.text4` |
| Uppercase section/column headers | `custom.colHead` |
| The one CTA, selection, focus, links, icon-hover | `primary.main` |
| Contained-button hover | `primary.dark` |
| Selected/tinted bg, focus ring, ID-chip bg | `custom.primaryBg` |
| Text/icon on a primary fill | `primary.contrastText` |
| Active / saved / online dot | `success.main` |
| Destructive action | `error.main` |
| Status swatch dots & ID-chip tints (decorative only) | `custom.status.*` |

Rules: **one** `primary` per surface (the CTA/selection accent) â€” everything else is `text-*`/`divider`. Status colors are **decoration only** (dots, chip tints), never interactive color. Dark-mode brightness/tinting is handled inside the theme's two palettes, so a correctly-sloted component needs zero per-mode code.

---

## 3. Layout

- **Full-height app:** column flex â€” menu row / ribbon / content (`flex: 1; minHeight: 0`) / status bar. Fixed bands `flexShrink: 0`.
- **Board:** horizontal-scroll flex row, `gap: 2` (16px), page padding `p: 2.5` (20px); columns `width: 296, flexShrink: 0`, internal column flex `gap: 1`.
- **List view:** two-pane flex row filling the space between ribbon and status bar â€” sidebar `width: 280, flexShrink: 0`, editor p

While the commit operation is running, the dialog is simply disabled. we should add some animation to show a process is running and include a little text to show what is occuring.

we just recently did something similar for merge I think, perhaps use similar style

## Current state

`PrimaryChangesDialog` opens when worktree integration finds changes in the primary project branch. `PrimaryChangesService.confirm` marks the service busy, calls `StorageService.commitPrimaryChanges`, and closes the dialog after success. `WorktreeService` then retries integration. A failed commit is reported through `dialogService`; the dialog remains open with the entered message so the user can retry.

The shared busy state covers both committing and moving a file to trash. It disables the OK and trash controls and makes Cancel a no-op, but it does not identify which operation is running. During a commit, the dialog shows no progress animation or status text, and the commit-message field remains editable. The merge-conflict dialog already uses the intended pattern: an informational alert with `CircularProgress`, explanatory text, and a progress state on the primary action.

## implementation details

* Add commit-specific state to `PrimaryChangesService`, separate from its generic busy state. Expose that state through a granular `EventTarget` event and a `useSyncExternalStore` hook. File-trash operations must remain busy without being presented as commits.
* Set commit-specific state immediately before `commitPrimaryChanges` starts. Clear it after failure, and reset it when the review finishes after success, cancellation, service reinitialization, or cleanup.
* While commit-specific state is active, show an informational alert in `PrimaryChangesDialog` with an accessible `CircularProgress` and text stating that project changes are being committed. Change the OK button label to `Committing...` and include a small spinner, matching the merge-conflict completion feedback.
* Disable the commit-message field, OK, Cancel, file-trash actions, backdrop close, and Escape close until the commit finishes. The commit is non-cancellable: after the storage call starts, dialog controls cannot stop it safely.
* Keep the dialog open while the commit promise is pending. On success, preserve current behavior: close the review, resolve it as confirmed, then let `WorktreeService` retry integration. On failure, remove progress feedback, keep the message and file list, report the existing error, and restore controls for retry.
* Add focused component tests with a deferred commit promise to verify immediate feedback, accessible progress, disabled controls, pending-dialog visibility, success closure, and failure recovery. Add service tests for commit-specific state and events. Keep storage and worktree integration contracts unchanged.

## acceptance criteria

* Starting a commit immediately shows a progress animation and text that identifies project changes as the operation in progress.
* While the commit is pending, the dialog stays open and no field, file action, button, backdrop click, or Escape key can start another action or close the review.
* Moving a file to trash does not show commit progress or the `Committing...` label.
* Successful commit closes the dialog, resolves the review as confirmed, and allows the existing integration retry to continue.
* Failed commit removes progress feedback, preserves the commit message and file list, reports the existing error, and permits retry or cancellation.
* Progress feedback is accessible and uses theme-backed MUI styling consistent with merge-conflict completion feedback.
* Focused `PrimaryChangesService` and `PrimaryChangesDialog` tests pass, and `npm run lint` passes.

The configuration dialog uses a **Role** dropdown. It should contain the legend items instead of the internal role definitions.

## Current state

The node details editor exposes the internal diagram roles, such as `focal`, `backend`, and `store`, in the **Role** dropdown. It also exposes the user-facing node legend items in a separate **Legend entry** dropdown. Both controls edit the same node classification.

The diagram model requires both `role` and `legendEntryId`. The existing legend-entry change handler already derives the compatible internal role or node kind and saves the complete classification through `setNodeClassification`.

## Implementation details

Replace the internal-role options in the **Role** dropdown with the node legend entries from `DiagramData.meta.legend`. Display each entry's label and use its `id` as the selected value.

When the user selects an entry, reuse the existing legend-entry change behavior to update `legendEntryId` and derive the compatible internal `role` or node `kind`. Keep the internal fields in the model, but do not expose their raw values in this dropdown. Remove the separate **Legend entry** dropdown because it would duplicate the same choice.

Keep the existing **Kind** control for flow diagrams and the existing atomic `setNodeClassification` save operation. Do not change edge configuration as part of this feature.

## Acceptance criteria

* The node configuration dialog's **Role** dropdown lists the user-facing labels of the diagram's node legend entries.
* Raw internal role values are not presented as dropdown options.
* The separate **Legend entry** dropdown is removed.
* Selecting a role-based legend entry updates both `legendEntryId` and `role`.
* Selecting a node-kind legend entry updates `legendEntryId` and the compatible node kind while preserving the node's role.
* Saving applies the classification as one operation, and cancelling leaves the node unchanged.
* Tests cover custom legend labels, role-based entries, node-kind entries, saving, and cancellation.

Check this trace: [Trace-typing.json](file:///C:/Users/janbo/Documents/dev/Trace-typing.json)

it is taken while typing in the markdown editor of a card. this is beginning to feel slugish. what is the system doing?

## Current state

The trace contains 39 keystrokes. One keystroke takes about 203 ms because a background worktree update schedules a synchronous React update at the same time. The remaining keystrokes take 2.8-5.9 ms each. Markdown serialization and link-selection updates occur for every editor change, but they are not the source of the visible pause.

The desktop worktree service periodically reads the primary repository and every linked worktree. It suppresses publication when the resulting `WorktreeState` is unchanged. The renderer also compares individual records and the primary status before dispatching scoped events. An unchanged refresh must therefore stop at the service boundary and must not schedule a React update.

`WorktreeSelector` subscribes to live worktree and persistence state through `useWorktreeSelectorState`. A relevant status change rerenders the complete selector controller even when its menu and dialogs are closed. The dialogs are already mounted only while open, but the subscription still belongs to a component that owns the button, menu, dialog state, and action handlers.

## Implementation details

Keep the existing no-op suppression and add regression coverage across both service boundaries. An unchanged desktop refresh must not notify bridge listeners. Applying an equivalent renderer state must preserve existing record references and must not dispatch `recordChanged`, `recordsChanged`, `primaryStatusChanged`, or the general `changed` event.

Move the always-active `useWorktreeSelectorState` subscription into a small status-button component. This component owns the derived label, tooltip, disabled state, worktree-change indicators, and button rendering. It receives only stable assignment data and the open callback.

Mount the menu and dialog controller only while the menu or a worktree dialog is open. That controller may subscribe to live worktree state while active so action availability and dialog data remain current. The parent selector must not receive changing worktree status as props or own the live subscription.

Do not change the Markdown editor update or persistence flow. The trace does not show an editor-side performance problem that justifies a separate buffering or serialization mechanism.

## Acceptance criteria

- A scheduled worktree refresh that produces no state change does not notify renderer listeners or schedule a React update.
- A worktree record change only notifies subscribers for that record. A primary-status change only notifies subscribers that use primary status.
- While the selector is closed, a relevant worktree update rerenders only the status-button component, not the menu or dialog controller.
- The menu and dialog controller subscribes while active and reflects worktree changes that occur after it opens.
- The worktree menu and dialogs retain their current behavior for assignment, commit, update, integration, unassignment, busy states, and errors.
- Typing in the Markdown editor while a worktree refresh completes no longer produces a long React task from `WorktreeSelector`.
- Focused service and component tests cover unchanged refreshes, scoped status updates, and opening the selector after a background update.

r handling updates `ProjectSnapshot.repositoryFiles` one path at a time and publishes `repositoryChanged`, but it does not publish the project-wide `changed` event consumed by `useProjectState`. Mounted editors therefore keep their previous file-search list. Changes involving other file extensions or folders are not forwarded by the desktop watcher, so the renderer cannot repair the list from those events.

## Implementation details

* In `desktop/src/project/project_files.js`, continue ignoring `.git`. Forward create and delete events for every repository path so structural changes involving any file extension or folder reach the renderer. Continue filtering content-only update events to Markdown, JSON, and text files. Keep the existing per-path settle timer for duplicate native events.
* Keep `ProjectWatchEvent` and the preload, local, and remote-control bridge contracts unchanged. A path is structurally changed when it is reported as removed or when it is absent from the repository list held before the event. This also handles a move, which the watcher reports as removal of the old path plus creation of the new path.
* Add a repository-list refresh timer to `ProjectLoading`. Each structural event cancels and restarts the timer. After 250 ms without another structural event, call `storage.listRepositoryFiles` once for the active project. This reset-on-change delay is the debounce period.
* Do not reload the repository list for a content-only change to a path already present in the list. Continue publishing granular `repositoryChanged` events so existing file-specific reloads still run.
* On a successful request, exclude agent instruction paths using the same rule as project loading, replace `ProjectSnapshot.repositoryFiles` with the returned sorted list through `ProjectState`, and publish `changed` only when the list differs. Mounted editors then receive the new snapshot and rebuild their file-search options.
* Clear the pending timer when project loading resets, fails, stops, or switches project. Associate each request with the project reference, project-load token, and refresh revision that started it. Ignore a result when the project changed or a newer refresh superseded it.
* If listing fails, keep the previous repository list, report the failure through the existing optional-project-load warning path, and allow a later structural event to retry.
* Add focused tests in `desktop/src/project/project_files.test.mjs`, `app/src/services/project/project_loading.test.ts`, and `app/src/services/project/project_state.node.test.ts`. Cover non-text structural events, 250 ms batching, no refresh for known-path content changes, add/remove/move bursts, stale results, project switches, failures, and snapshot replacement. Existing Markdown editor file-search tests continue to verify that a new snapshot reaches the plugin.

## Acceptance criteria

* Adding, moving, or deleting a repository file of any extension causes the active repository file list to be requested after 250 ms without another structural event.
* Adding, moving, or deleting a folder causes the same refresh, so all contained repository paths are reflected.
* Multiple structural events within one 250 ms window produce one `listRepositoryFiles` request after the last event.
* Editing contents of a file already present in the repository list does not request a repository-list refresh.
* Successful refresh replaces the list atomically; `@` file autocomplete in an already mounted Markdown editor shows added and moved paths and stops showing deleted paths without reopening the project or editor.
* Agent instruction paths remain excluded from autocomplete after refresh, matching initial project loading.
* A refresh result from an old project or an older refresh request never changes the active project snapshot.
* A failed refresh leaves the previous list usable, reports a warning, and does not stop later structural events from scheduling another refresh.
* Existing Markdown, JSON, action, schedule, and agent-instruction watcher behavior remains unchanged.

---
author:
id: F_473
internalId: a7d96183-9b8a-4c2e-a51a-925f7ca9aded
title: tabbed lazy file diff workspace
status: ready
type: feature
owner:
affects:
agents:
  - design/releases/0.12.0/card__a7d96183-9b8a-4c2e-a51a-925f7ca9aded.json
policy:
after: 08b55903-731a-4a0d-be87-6818029c82b2
changedFiles:
  - .tmp/f473/desktop_tests.py
  - .tmp/f473/dispatch_tests.py
  - .tmp/f473/remove_config.py
  - app/src/components/card_view/card_commit_diff_panel.test.tsx
  - app/src/components/card_view/card_commit_diff_panel.tsx
  - app/src/components/card_view/diff_workspace/commit_diff_workspace_source.ts
  - app/src/components/card_view/diff_workspace/diff_workspace.tsx
  - app/src/components/card_view/diff_workspace/diff_workspace_file_tab.tsx
  - app/src/components/card_view/diff_workspace/diff_workspace_files_tab.tsx
  - app/src/components/card_view/diff_workspace/diff_workspace_search_button.tsx
  - app/src/components/card_view/diff_workspace/diff_workspace_search_row.tsx
  - app/src/components/card_view/diff_workspace/diff_workspace_search_service.test.ts
  - app/src/components/card_view/diff_workspace/diff_workspace_search_service.ts
  - app/src/components/card_view/diff_workspace/diff_workspace_service.node.test.ts
  - app/src/components/card_view/diff_workspace/diff_workspace_service.ts
  - app/src/components/card_view/diff_workspace/diff_workspace_tabs.tsx
  - app/src/components/card_view/diff_workspace/diff_workspace_types.ts
  - app/src/components/card_view/diff_workspace/worktree_diff_workspace_source.ts
  - app/src/services/data/diff_service.node.test.ts
  - app/src/services/data/diff_service.ts
  - desktop/src/git/diff_service.js
---

## Problem

The card diff panel currently renders the card body first, lists the other changed files, and then renders the complete multi-file patch when a file is selected. `DiffView.initialPath` only scrolls to that file; it does not limit loading or rendering to it. Worktree diff generation also reads and builds patches for every changed file before the file list becomes available.

This makes large commits and worktrees slow, and the selected file is difficult to find in a long vertical view.

## Decision

Keep the existing `CardBodyPopover` and list-view diff containers. Their header, footer, resizing, stacking, focus, mobile, and exit behavior already fit this feature. Do not add another popup type.

Replace the current diff-panel body with a tabbed workspace. Keep the existing read-only `MarkdownEditor` diff presentation for the card file; other file tabs use `react-diff-view`. The workspace owns navigation, lazy loading, and search while the surrounding popup remains unchanged.

## Tabs

* The first tab is always `Files` and is initially active.
* `Files` shows every changed file as a full repository-relative path. A rename is shown as `old/path -> new/path`.
* Selecting a file opens its tab and activates it. Selecting an already-open file activates the existing tab.
* A file tab label is only the filename and extension. Its tooltip and accessible label contain the full path so duplicate filenames remain distinguishable.
* The full path, not the short label, is the tab key and file-selection reference.
* Tabs scroll horizontally when they no longer fit. File tabs are not closable in this feature.
* Open tabs and the active tab reset when the diff source changes or the user exits diff mode.

## Lazy loading

Opening the workspace loads only the changed-file manifest needed by the `Files` tab. It does not load file contents or build patches.

Activating a file tab requests that file's diff. No other file is prefetched. A successfully loaded file may remain cached for the lifetime of that workspace so returning to its tab is immediate. Loading, empty, binary, unavailable, and error states apply to the active file only.

So lets first analyze what exactly is done when user assigns and then the second operation, updates the worktree. Are there any places where we could improve.

secondly, we will need to show some feedback to the user that the operation is in progress. maybe by a spinning border? we already have something similar for the 'run' button.

## Current state

`WorktreeSelector` awaits `WorktreeService` for assignment and update. `WorktreeService` marks the card as preparing, which disables the selector, but the closed menu leaves only a static disabled button. User gets no clear progress signal.

Assignment calls desktop `WorktreeService.prepare`. It lists and inspects every linked worktree, validates the selected worktree twice, checks or creates the card branch, switches the checkout, then refreshes primary and every linked worktree again. Desktop profile covers 24.9 seconds: 94.3% is idle waiting and child-process spawn is the largest active sample. Delay therefore comes mainly from waiting on many Git subprocesses, not desktop JavaScript computation.

Update first flushes pending app saves, then repeats repository-wide discovery and duplicate selected-worktree validation before checkpointing primary changes, rebasing, and refreshing every worktree. A checkpoint is an automatic local commit of pending primary-worktree changes. Renderer trace also contains React tasks up to 231 ms; broad worktree `changed` events currently wake every selector subscription when one card starts or finishes an operation.

## implementation details

- Keep branch naming, reservation checks, repository-identity checks, clean-worktree checks, pending-save flush, primary checkpoint, rebase/conflict handling, persistence, and error behavior unchanged.
- In desktop assignment and update, start from the selected cached branch record, verify repository identity, branch, and status once, then operate on that record. Do not list or inspect unrelated worktrees before the operation. Leave shared `requireClean` behavior unchanged for its other callers.

# MD² 0.12.0

## New features

* View and edit JSON files in a dedicated editor.
* Browse changed files in tabs and add inline review comments.
* Choose whether to keep a local project's design folder out of Git.
* Open email links in your default email app.
* Choose which actions to show, including those with conversation history.
* Configure diagram items using legend labels.
* Select nested lists and starting positions for for-each actions.
* Track for-each progress, resume from a stopped position, and advance step by step.
* Control how often for-each actions compact or start a new conversation.
* Include the full current record in a for-each prompt.

## Improvements and fixes

* Improved JSON editing, worktree operations, and feedback during project integration.
* Remember a separate window size for code diffs.
* Updated documentation and improved Markdown editor responsiveness.
* Fixed issues with project switching, file links, action conversations, and for-each runs.
* File suggestions now reflect added, moved, and deleted files.

# Running actions

![Board with a card popup and the action popup open](../screenshots/Screenshot%202026-07-23%20180206.jpg)

## Entry points

Actions show up next to the thing they act on, filtered by their `appliesTo`:

- **Run** button and the overflow menu on a card;
- the card popup toolbar;
- the file tree context menu, for files and folders;
- the editor toolbar in list view;
- the **Run** tab of the application menu, for project-level actions;
- the Diagrams view, for root diagrams and actions on selected diagram items.

Activating any of them opens the action popup for that action and context.

## The action popup

The popup is resizable and shows the action label, its description, run controls, live status, the log for the current phase, and previous runs. Linked `onBefore` and `onAfter` actions appear as chips â€” click one to open it with the same context.

For agent actions you also get:

- a prompt box for run-specific input ({% raw %}`{{card-prompt}}`{% endraw %});
- agent, account, model, and reasoning-level selectors, prefilled from the definition and the defaults. Changing them affects this run only, never the definition;
- phrase buttons, if the action defines `phrases`;
- **Convert to action**, which turns a custom prompt you just wrote into a reusable action definition.

Buttons: **Run** starts the chain. **Cancel** stops the running process and the rest of the chain. **Schedule** runs it later (see below).

While an action runs for a card, that card's entry points are disabled â€” one action at a time per card. This state is in memory only, so nothing is left disabled after a restart.

When agent task tracking is enabled, a running card shows a progress bar below its **Run** button as soon as the agent publishes a non-empty task list. Hover the bar for the completed and total counts; assistive technology receives the same context from its accessible name. The task list also appears in the action popup and conversation panel. Incomplete lists open expanded; fully completed lists open collapsed, with their completed/total count still visible. You can expand or collapse them manually.

## Conversations

In list view, the conversation panel attaches to the active file or
[19037 characters omitted]
 column. That is how one **Run** button does the right thing in every column.

The action names above are examples. Write your own in the action editor, or start from the [Cookbook](../actions/cookbook.md).

## 1. Create and describe

1. Press **+** on the `new` column.
2. Pick a type (feature, job, bug) and type a title.
3. Write what you want in the body. Rough is fine: a few bullet points.

mdÂ² creates a Markdown file in the working folder, for example `F_12_my_feature.md`, and commits it after the auto-commit delay.

Reference: [Your first card](../getting-started/your-first-card.md), [Cards and files](../concepts/cards-and-files.md).

## 2. Use the editor

Click the card to open the card popup, or **Open in file mode** to edit it in a list view tab.

- The formatting toolbar handles bold, lists, links, images, tables, and code blocks.
- **Affects** lists the repository files the card touches, with suggestions as you type. The list is stored in the card header, where agents reading the card see it.
- The card menu holds policy toggles (named flags such as "needs review"), worktree assignment, and delete.
- In list view, **Properties** shows the header fields and **Agents** opens the conversation panel beside the document.

Edits are saved to the file and committed after you stop typing.

Reference: [Board view](../guide/board-view.md), [List view](../guide/text-view.md).

## 3. Design with an agent

Drag the card to `design` and press **Run**. The action popup opens with the column's default action selected.

1. Add run-specific instructions in the prompt box if you want. They reach the prompt through {% raw %}`{{card-prompt}}`{% endraw %}.
2. Check the agent, account, model, and reasoning level. Changes here apply to this run only.
3. Press **Run**.

For a streaming action, the conversation stays open: answer the agent's questions, then press **Finish**. An action with `autoFinish` finishes by itself when the agent moves the card to the configured column.

Read the result in the card. Edit it until it says what you want.

Reference: [Running actions](../actions/running-actions.md), [Actions and agents](../concepts/actions-and-agents.md).

## 4. Implement

Drag the card to `ready for implementation` and press **Run** again. For parallel work, assign a worktree first; see [Git worktrees](git-worktrees.md).

While the agent runs, the card shows **Running** and its other action entry points are disabled. One action at a time per card. If the agent publishes a task list, a progress bar below **Run** shows how many tasks are complete.

## 5. Follow the conversation

The conversation belongs to the card. Open it from the card's conversation icon, from the action popup's previous runs, or with **Agents** in list view.

- Send a next turn to steer the agent.
- Use phrase buttons, if the action defines them, for replies you type often.
- Pick another agent mid-conversation; mdÂ² migrates the conversation.

Logs are stored in the `activity` folder and stay attached to the card.

## 6. Review the result

- **Commits**: the commit icon in the card popup lists the commits made during runs, each with its diff.
- **Review action**: run an agent that checks the implementation against the card. Move problems to `to fix` and run the fix action.
- **Usage**: token usage per run and per card; **Stats** compares cards and actions.

Reference: [Git and commits](../guide/git-and-commits.md), [Stats](../guide/stats.md).

## 7. Release

When the cards in `ready` are done, **Complete release** on the **Run** tab of the menu asks for a release name and moves every active card into a new subfolder of the releases folder, leaving the board empty for the next cycle. Cards you want gone without releasing them go to the archive instead.

Reference: [Release process](../contributing/release-process.md), [Project layout](../concepts/project-layout.md).

## Next

[Git worktrees](git-worktrees.md) or [Sequencing and scheduling cards](sequencing-and-scheduling.md).

# MDÂ² 0.12.0

## New features

* View and edit JSON files in a dedicated editor.
* Browse changed files in tabs and add inline review comments.
* Choose whether to keep a local project's design folder out of Git.
* Open email links in your default email app.
* Choose which actions to show, including those with conversation history.
* Configure diagram items using legend labels.
* Select nested lists and starting positions for for-each actions.
* Track for-each progress, resume from a stopped position, and advance step by step.
* Control how often for-each actions compact or start a new conversation.
* Include the full current record in a for-each prompt.

## Improvements and fixes

* Improved JSON editing, worktree operations, and feedback during project integration.
* Remember a separate window size for code diffs.
* Updated documentation and improved Markdown editor responsiveness.
* Fixed issues with project switching, file links, action conversations, and for-each runs.
* File suggestions now reflect added, moved, and deleted files.

we recently added the 'for-each' functionality, see ( )

This is working, but we now need to add some progress indicator so that the user can see how far along we are in the list.

This should be a horizontal progress indicator (thin) just above the 'tasks' list.

We already have a progress indicator on the 'run' button on the action-cards. This should also indicate the progress in the for-each list.

## Current state

`ActionRun.executeAgentForEach` resolves the complete record list and processes it sequentially, so the desktop runner knows the current record index and total count. It does not publish this information.

`ActionRunRegistry` consequently has no loop-level progress state. The existing run-button indicator derives its value from the active agent conversation's task list, which describes work within one conversation and resets when a for-each run starts another conversation. The action popup renders this task list without a for-each progress indicator.

## Implementation details

Add a granular `forEachProgress` action-run update containing `processedCount` and `totalCount`. Publish `0/total` before the first record starts and publish an updated value after every processed record, including a failed record when the failure policy continues the loop.

Store the latest progress on the corresponding run in `ActionRunRegistry`. Clear it when the outer run becomes terminal; the final run event remains the authority for completion, failure, or cancellation.

Add a thin determinate progress indicator to the action conversation directly above `AgentTaskList`. Show it only for the active for-each run. Update the existing run-button indicator to prefer for-each progress while it is present and retain the current agent-task progress for ordinary runs.

- Pressing `Send` continues the current record with the entered prompt and does not change the record index.

When we stop a for-each, we continue to show the progress bar. this is ok, but the position is lost, we should keep this so we can find the last position easier again

## Current state

`ActionRun.executeAgentForEach` publishes `forEachProgress` before the first selected record and after each processed record. Cancellation does not count the interrupted record as processed, so the last published `processedCount` already identifies the next start index.

`ActionRunRegistry` stores this progress while the run is active, but clears it for every terminal status, including `cancelled`. The popup progress indicator reads only this live run value. The conversation persists its for-each configuration, but not its progress, so the position is unavailable after cancellation, run-store release, or reopening the conversation.

## Implementation details

- Add optional `forEachProgress` to the canonical `AgentConversation` and validate `processedCount` and `totalCount` as safe non-negative integers with `processedCount <= totalCount`.
- When a for-each run is cancelled, persist its latest published progress on the active conversation before publishing the terminal run event. The persisted value must remain the count of completed records; the interrupted record is not completed.
- Preserve cancelled for-each progress in `ActionRunRegistry`. Continue clearing transient interaction state and clear progress for successful completion and other terminal outcomes.
- Update `ForEachProgressIndicator` to use live run progress first and the selected persisted conversation progress otherwise. Do not change the run-button behavior, which shows progress only while a run is active.
- Keep progress scoped to its conversation and run. Starting another run must not reuse progress from a previously cancelled run.
- Add focused tests for activity persistence and parsing, cancellation ordering, registry terminal handling, and live-to-historical popup rendering.

## Acceptance criteria

- Stopping a non-empty for-each run leaves the popup progress bar at the last completed-record count.
- A record interrupted by Stop is not counted as processed. The displayed `processedCount` is the zero-based start index to use when resuming with the first unprocessed record.
- The stopped position remains available after closing and reopening the conversation and after reloading the project.
- Progress that starts from a non-zero `startIndex` retains that initial offset after cancellation.
- Completed records and failed records handled by `logAndContinue` count as processed before a later cancellation.
- Successful completion and non-cancellation failure retain their current terminal behavior and do not leave historical for-each progress visible.
- Ordinary actions and empty for-each runs do not show a for-each progress bar.
- Progress from one conversation or run never appears on another conversation or run.

The `for-each` feature is commercially valuable but effectively invisible on the current website. It deserves both landing-page exposure and a dedicated documentation page.

## What the feature offers

Based on the [0.11.0 release notes](C:/Users/janbo/Documents/dev/md2/design/releases/0.11.0/release_notes.md:9), [0.12.0 release notes](C:/Users/janbo/Documents/dev/md2/design/releases/0_12_0/release_notes.md:15), and related designs, users can:

- Run one agent action sequentially across JSON records.
- Insert the complete record with `{{data}}` or selected values with `{{data path}}`.
- Select a nested array from a root JSON object.
- Reuse one conversation, periodically compact it, or start new conversations in batches.
- Continue after failures or stop immediately.
- Track progress, restart at a chosen index, and retain the stopped position.
- Automatically advance or inspect records step by step.

The clearest commercial framing is:

> Turn structured data into controlled agent work. Attach a JSON dataset and run the same focused action for every record—with progress, failure handling, resumability, and control over conversation boundaries.

This speaks to scalability and reliability without overstating the feature as general workflow automation. It is currently run-specific and only available for agent conversations in the action popup, not stored in action definitions ([design constraint](C:/Users/janbo/Documents/dev/md2/design/releases/0.11.0/F_458_add_for_each_feature.md:78)).

## Best website placements

1. **Repository landing page — highest commercial value**

   Add a section immediately after “Reusable, controlled actions” in [README.md](C:/Users/janbo/Documents/dev/md2/README.md:89). This is where visitors are already learning why actions matter.

   Suggested heading: “Run one action across structured data.”

   Keep this benefit-led: eliminate repetitive prompt setup, retain control over context, monitor progress, and resume interrupted work. Include one short example such as reviewing endpoints, migrating modules, or generating documentation from an inventory.

2. **Dedicated documentation page — essential**

   Create `docs/actions/for-each.md`. The feature has enough behavior and operational choices that inserting everything into another page would make it hard to understand.

   It should cover:

   - Attaching and replacing a JSON file.
   - Root arrays, root objects, and nested-list selection.
   - `{{data}}` and `{{data path}}`.
   - Add Prompt, Compact, and New Conversation modes.
   - Records per batch.
   - Failure policies.
   - Start index, progress, stopping, and resuming.
   - Step-by-step mode and the Next/Send/Stop distinctions.
   - Invalid JSON, missing paths, empty arrays, and cancellation.

3. **Documentation homepage — discoverability**

   Add the new guide to “Actions reference” in [docs/README.md](C:/Users/janbo/Documents/dev/md2/docs/README.md:54). The existing summary currently lists action definitions, placeholders, running actions, agent setup, and the cookbook, but gives no indication that actions can process datasets.

4. **Running Actions — workflow entry point**

   Add a concise “Run an action for each JSON record” section after “The action popup” in [running-actions.md](C:/Users/janbo/Documents/dev/md2/docs/actions/running-actions.md:18). Explain where the menu item is and the basic run flow, then link to the dedicated guide.

5. **Placeholder reference — factual gap**

   Add `{{data}}` and `{{data path}}` to [placeholders.md](C:/Users/janbo/Documents/dev/md2/docs/actions/placeholders.md:5), including:

   - Full-record versus field selection.
   - Dot-separated object keys and numeric array indexes.
   - Value formatting.
   - The error when used outside a for-each record.

6. **Cookbook — practical conversion**

   Add a “Process a JSON dataset” recipe to [cookbook.md](C:/Users/janbo/Documents/dev/md2/docs/actions/cookbook.md:7). Because the attachment is run-specific, the recipe should provide an action prompt containing the data placeholders and then explain how to attach the JSON at runtime.

7. **Visual proof**

   Add a short video or screenshot showing JSON attachment, setup, and progress. Place it in the landing-page Videos or Screenshots area. A visible `3/20` progress state communicates the feature faster than configuration prose.

The action-definition page, scheduling section, and first-card onboarding are poor primary placements: for-each is not action-definition configuration, is distinct from card sequences, and is too advanced for the initial ten-minute workflow.

## Prioritized task list

### P0 — Complete the documentation

- Create `docs/actions/for-each.md` with the complete workflow and edge cases.
- Update `docs/actions/placeholders.md` for `{{data}}` and `{{data path}}`.
- Add a short for-each section and guide link to `docs/actions/running-actions.md`.
- Add the new page to the Actions reference table in `docs/README.md`.
- Verify every description against the current UI, especially start index, records per batch, step-by-step behavior, and retained cancellation progress.

### P1 — Add commercial discovery

- Add a benefit-led section to the root `README.md` after “Reusable, controlled actions.”
- Use “data-driven agent runs” or “run one action across structured data” as the customer-facing terminology.
- Mention three concrete use cases without implying parallel execution.
- Add a direct “Learn about for-each actions” link to the new guide.
- Capture a screenshot or short video showing attachment, setup, and progress.

### P2 — Improve adoption

- Add a cookbook recipe using both full-record and field placeholders.
- Provide a small downloadable sample JSON dataset and example prompt.
- Cross-link the guide from “Actions and agents.”
- Check rendered Jekyll navigation, raw Liquid handling around placeholders, link validity, and mobile screenshot readability.

No files were changed.

entries.content:
# Run an action for each JSON record

For-each runs the same agent action over a JSON dataset. Attach the data when you open an action, then let mdÂ² process its records in order while it tracks progress and keeps every result with the conversation.

Use it for repeated work driven by structured data, such as reviewing a list of endpoints, updating several modules, checking repository findings, or producing one result for every item in an inventory.

For-each is available for agent actions in the action popup. It is run-specific: the JSON data and settings belong to the draft or conversation, not to the reusable action definition.

## Attach JSON data

1. Open an agent action.
2. Open the prompt menu beside the prompt box.
3. Choose **For each** and select one `.json` file.
4. Write or select a prompt that uses the current record, then run the action.

After attachment, the loop icon appears beside the prompt menu. Its tooltip shows the selected file name. Open it to **View** the saved JSON, **Remove** it, or change the loop **Setup**.

mdÂ² saves the parsed JSON with the draft or conversation. Viewing or continuing the run does not depend on the original file remaining in place. Selecting another valid JSON file replaces the current attachment; an invalid file leaves the existing configuration unchanged.

## Choose the records

A root JSON array is the record list:

```json
[
  { "method": "GET", "path": "/users" },
  { "method": "POST", "path": "/users" }
]
```

A root object is one record by default. If the object contains the list you want, open **Setup** and set **Path to list data**:

```json
{
  "api": {
    "endpoints": [
      { "method": "GET", "path": "/users" },
      { "method": "POST", "path": "/users" }
    ]
  }
}
```

For this example, use `api.endpoints`. Selectors use dot-separated object keys and zero-based array indexes, so a path such as `groups.0.endpoints` can traverse an array inside the object. The selected value must be an array.

An empty root array or selected array completes without starting an agent turn. A root object without a selector runs once with that object as the record.

## Use the current record in a prompt

{% raw %}

| Placeholder | Value |
| --- | --- |
| `{{data}}` | The complete current record as pretty-printed JSON. |
| `{{data path}}` | The value at a dot-separated path in the current record, such as `{{data path}}` or `{{data owner.name}}`. Numeric segments select array items. |

For the endpoint data above, an action prompt could be:

```text
Review this endpoint for missing validation and authorization checks:

{{data}}

Pay particular attention to the {{data method}} request at {{data path}}.
```

Strings selected by a path are inserted as plain text. Numbers, booleans, `null`, objects, and arrays are inserted as JSON. A missing path fails that record according to the selected failure policy.

Data placeholders require an active for-each record. Using one in an ordinary run fails before the agent starts.

{% endraw %}

## Configure the loop

Open the loop icon and choose **Setup**.

| Setting | Behavior |
| --- | --- |
| **At end: Add prompt** | Keep one conversation and add every later record as another prompt. This is the default. |
| **At end: Compact** | Keep one conversation and compact it after each full batch when more records remain. |
| **At end: New conversation** | Start a new conversation for each batch. |
| **Records per batch** | Number of consecutive records that share a conversation before Compact or New conversation applies. |
| **On failure: Log and continue** | Record the failure and continue with the next record. This is the default. |
| **On failure: Stop on first failure** | Record the failure and do not start later records. |
| **Start index** | Zero-based position of the first record to process. Use `2` to start with the third record. |
| **Step by step** | Pause after each completed record so you can continue it, advance with **Next**, or stop. |
| **Path to list data** | For a root object, select the nested array to process. |

**Records per batch** is available for Compact and New conversation. Batch counting starts at the configured start index. Add prompt always keeps one conversation, so the batch value does not affect it.

Setup changes are disabled while the loop is running.

## Monitor, stop, and resume

A determinate progress bar in the action popup and on the card's action button shows completed records against the total. Records handled by **Log and continue** count as processed after their failure is recorded.

**Stop** cancels the active turn and prevents all remaining records from starting. The popup retains the completed-record count after cancellation, including after reopening the conversation. To resume, enter that count as the **Start index** and run the action again. An interrupted record is not counted as completed.

With **Step by step** disabled, mdÂ² advances automatically after a record completes. With it enabled:

- **Send** continues the current record with another prompt;
- **Next** finishes the current record and starts the next one; and
- **Stop** cancels the current work and all remaining records.

When the agent has a pending question or approval, answer it before advancing. **Next** stays disabled while that interaction is unresolved.

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | What to check |
| --- | --- |
| The file is rejected | The selected file must have a `.json` name and contain valid JSON. |
| The object runs only once | Set **Path to list data** to the array inside the root object. |
| Setup reports that the path is not a list | The selected path exists but does not resolve to an array. |
| A record reports a missing data path | Check the path used by the selector or prompt against that record's shape. |
| No agent turn starts | The selected list may be empty, or the start index may be at or beyond its length. |
| A stopped run starts from the beginning | Set **Start index** to the completed-record count shown by the retained progress bar. |

For-each records run sequentially. The feature requires the desktop execution backend and does not run in web-only GitHub mode.

See also: [Running actions](running-actions.md), [Placeholders](placeholders.md), [Actions and agents](../concepts/actions-and-agents.md).

* We recently introduced a new feature: `editable json data view`
* Read the release notes and design docs about this feature
* search for the best places on the website to add some relevant, commercial info regarding this new feature.
* report back and prepare a task list for improving the website about this new feature.

I’m using the technical-writer skill because this is a documentation-to-commercial-messaging audit. I’ll first trace the feature through release/design docs, then inspect the website’s existing content structure and report prioritized placement opportunities with a concrete task list—without changing files.

---
name: technical-writer
description: "Use this agent when you need to create, improve, or maintain technical documentation including API references, user guides, SDK documentation, and getting-started guides."
tools: Read, Write, Edit, Glob, Grep, WebFetch, WebSearch
model: haiku
---

You are a senior technical writer with expertise in creating comprehensive, user-friendly documentation. Your focus spans API references, user guides, tutorials, and technical content with emphasis on clarity, accuracy, and helping users succeed with technical products and services.


When invoked:
1. Query context manager for documentation needs and audience
2. Review existing documentation, product features, and user feedback
3. Analyze content gaps, clarity issues, and improvement opportunities
4. Create documentation that empowers users and reduces support burden

Technical writing checklist:
- Readability score > 60 achieved
- Technical accuracy 100% verified
- Examples provided comprehensively
- Visuals included appropriately
- Version controlled properly
- Peer reviewed thoroughly
- SEO optimized effectively
- User feedback positive consistently

Documentation types:
- Developer documentation
- End-user guides
- Administrator manuals
- API references
- SDK documentation
- Integration guides
- Best practices
- Troubleshooting guides

Content creation:
- Information architecture
- Content planning
- Writing standards
- Style consistency
- Terminology management
- Version control
- Review processes
- Publishing workflows

API documentation:
- Endpoint descriptions
- Parameter documentation
- Request/response examples

check this trace: [Trace-scroll.json](file:///C:/Users/janbo/Documents/dev/Trace-scroll.json)

this is of a single scroll. the render takes very long. what is it doing? how can we improve?

## Current state

`JsonArrayEditor` uses `TableVirtuoso`. Its scroll handler updates Virtuoso's external store through `flushSync`; when the visible range changes, Virtuoso synchronously replaces the rendered row window. The trace contains one such range refresh after the recorded scroll. It is not caused by `JsonDataDocument`, file loading, or document change events.

The refresh creates 38 rows with 15 data columns: 608 table cells and 532 `JsonScalarEditor` instances. Virtualized body cells use MUI components such as `TableCell`, `TextField`, `Checkbox`, and `Link`. Mounting these components runs Emotion insertion effects. Two `StyleSheet._insertTag` calls consume about 825 ms of the 1.42-second refresh; React development instrumentation adds further overhead.

Continued scrolling repeats the row-window replacement whenever the visible range advances. Row memoization cannot prevent work for rows that Virtuoso unmounts and replaces.

## implementation details

* Configure `TableVirtuoso` with scroll-seek mode. Use named enter and exit velocity constants and render lightweight placeholder table rows while scrolling. Exit scroll-seek mode only after velocity falls below the exit threshold, then render the final visible range once.
* Add a dedicated scroll-seek row component. Render native `tr` and `td` elements, preserve the measured row height and full column span, and do not mount cell editors, selection controls, links, or MUI components in placeholders.
* Remove Emotion-backed components from the virtualized body-row hot path. Add array-specific body cells and a scalar editor using semantic native table and form elements. Apply table-body styling through stable classes whose theme-dependent rules are inserted once outside the virtualized rows. Keep the MUI header and footer because they are not replaced during scrolling.
* Preserve existing value handling. String and boolean edits still update `JsonDataDocument` immediately; number edits keep the existing draft, validation, blur, Enter, and Escape behavior; missing object fields still create the field; nested values still drill into the document.
* Keep the shared `JsonScalarEditor` unchanged for object and root-value editing. Do not add a behavior flag to it; the lightweight editor belongs to the array table only.
* Preserve column widths, horizontal overflow, selected-row highlighting, accessibility names, read-only behavior, and row operation ordering. Scrolling must not publish a `JsonDataDocument` change.
* Add focused tests for the array-specific scalar controls and placeholder row, and retain the existing array editing, virtualization, resizing, selection, nested-value, and read-only coverage. Verify the fix with a development performance trace and run the focused JSON editor tests and app lint.

## acceptance criteria

* Active fast scrolling renders lightweight placeholder rows instead of repeatedly mounting complete editable rows. The final visible rows become editable after scrolling settles.
* Repeated virtual-range changes do not add Emotion styles from body cells and do not produce recurring `StyleSheet._insertTag` blocks attributable to the JSON array body.
* Scrolling does not reload JSON data, publish document changes, change dirty state, selection, column widths, or the current JSON location.
* Strings, numbers, booleans, nulls, missing fields, and nested values retain their existing editing and navigation behavior in editable and read-only documents.
* Column resizing, header/body alignment, horizontal scrolling, row selection, and add, delete, copy, cut, and paste operations continue to work.
* Focused JSON editor tests and app lint pass.

# MDÂ² 0.12.0

## New features

* View and edit JSON files in a dedicated editor.
* Browse changed files in tabs and add inline review comments.
* Choose whether to keep a local project's design folder out of Git.
* Open email links in your default email app.
* Choose which actions to show, including those with conversation history.
* Configure diagram items using legend labels.
* Select nested lists and starting positions for for-each actions.
* Track for-each progress, resume from a stopped position, and advance step by step.
* Control how often for-each actions compact or start a new conversation.
* Include the full current record in a for-each prompt.

## Improvements and fixes

* Improved JSON editing, worktree operations, and feedback during project integration.
* Remember a separate window size for code diffs.
* Updated documentation and improved Markdown editor responsiveness.
* Fixed issues with project switching, file links, action conversations, and for-each runs.
* File suggestions now reflect added, moved, and deleted files.

we just introduced the new json editor. it contains an object editor which shows 2 columns: the fieldname: field value (can be a button.

* first, show the button as links
* add a header
* show in a table style, so horizontal row indicators
* the column resizer jumps back to the original position first when you want to resize, so it is poorly implemented
* the column divider should be a thin line, the drag area may be wider
* the field-value inputs should use the remaining width of the value column

## Current state

`JsonObjectEditor` renders object properties in a two-column CSS grid without column headers or horizontal row dividers. Nested object and array values use outlined `Open ...` buttons, so navigation controls look heavier than inline values. Scalar inputs keep their intrinsic width instead of filling the remaining value-column space.

The field-name splitter uses the pointer's absolute position inside the editor to calculate column width. Container padding and grid gaps are included in that position but not in the stored width, so the column jumps when dragging starts. The full six-pixel drag target is also painted as the divider, which makes the visible line too heavy.

## implementation details

* Keep object fields in one resizable two-column layout. Add a header row labelled `Field` and `Value`, and separate header and data rows with one-pixel horizontal `divider` lines so the form reads like a table.
* Render nested object and array drill-in controls as link-style text buttons: buttons with hyperlink styling, not URL anchors. Keep their current `document.drillInto` navigation, labels, keyboard access, and focus behavior.
* On pointer down, store both pointer X position and current field-name width. During movement, add pointer delta to stored width, then clamp against existing minimum field and value widths. Pointer up, cancellation, and lost capture end the same bounded drag session.
* Keep a wider splitter hit target for pointer and touch input, but draw a centered one-pixel divider inside it. Use theme `divider` color at rest and `primary.main` for hover, focus, and active states.
* Make `TextField` controls fill the value column's available width. Preserve the minimum value-column width and allow controls to shrink with the editor without causing horizontal overflow. Keep checkbox controls at their natural size.
* Extend `json_data_editor.test.tsx` with object header, link-style drill-in, no-jump pointer resize, and clamping coverage. Keep existing keyboard resize and breadcrumb navigation behavior. Verify divider thickness, hit-target width, hover, focus, active state, and light and dark themes manually because these are visual styling requirements.

## acceptance criteria

* Object editor shows `Field` and `Value` headers above property rows.
* Each object property row has a horizontal divider, using theme colors in light and dark modes.
* Nested object and array values appear as link-style controls and still open the selected value by pointer or keyboard.
* Starting a drag from any point in splitter hit target keeps current column width until pointer moves; movement changes width only by pointer movement distance.
* Pointer resizing cannot make field-name column narrower than its minimum or leave value column narrower than its minimum. Keyboard resizing keeps same bounds.
* Splitter presents a one-pixel visible divider while retaining wider pointer and touch hit target. Hover, keyboard focus, and active drag remain visible.
* String, number, and null `TextField` controls use all available value-column width and shrink with the editor without horizontal overflow.
* Focused JSON editor tests and `npm run lint` pass.

Setup changes are disabled while the loop is running.

## Monitor, stop, and resume

A determinate progress bar in the action popup and on the card's action button shows completed records against the total. Records handled by **Log and continue** count as processed after their failure is recorded.

**Stop** cancels the active turn and prevents all remaining records from starting. The popup retains the completed-record count after cancellation, including after reopening the conversation. To resume, enter that count as the **Start index** and run the action again. An interrupted record is not counted as completed.

With **Step by step** disabled, mdÂ² advances automatically after a record completes. With it enabled:

- **Send** continues the current record with another prompt;
- **Next** finishes the current record and starts the next one; and
- **Stop** cancels the current work and all remaining records.

When the agent has a pending question or approval, answer it before advancing. **Next** stays disabled while that interaction is unresolved.

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | What to check |
| --- | --- |
| The file is rejected | The selected file must have a `.json` name and contain valid JSON. |
| The object runs only once | Set **Path to list data** to the array inside the root object. |
| Setup reports that the path is not a list | The selected path exists but does not resolve to an array. |
| A record reports a missing data path | Check the path used by the selector or prompt against that record's shape. |
| No agent turn starts | The selected list may be empty, or the start index may be at or beyond its length. |
| A stopped run starts from the beginning | Set **Start index** to the completed-record count shown by the retained progress bar. |

For-each records run sequentially. The feature requires the desktop execution backend and does not run in web-only GitHub mode.

See also: [Running actions](running-actions.md), [Placeholders](placeholders.md), [Actions and agents](../concepts/actions-and-agents.md).

# Open your first project

A project is a Git repository with a folder mdÂ² manages. Any repository works â€” an existing codebase is the normal case.

## Desktop app

1. Menu â†’ **Open project**.
2. Pick a folder that contains a `.git` directory.
3. If mdÂ² finds no project folder, it offers to create one. Accept the default (`design`) or type another name.
4. If the project folder exists but has no working folder, mdÂ² asks which folder holds your cards, or creates one.

mdÂ² then creates what it needs and loads the board. A spinner and the project name in the app bar show progress; large histories load in the background.

The last project reopens automatically next time you start.

## Web, against GitHub

1. Click the GitHub button in the upper right and follow the link to create a personal access token with repository access, then paste it in.
2. Menu â†’ **Open project**, source **GitHub**.
3. Pick the repository from the list, or type owner and repository and press **Load branches**.
4. Choose a branch and press **Open**.

Cards can be created and edited; actions and agents are not available in this mode. See [Storage modes](../concepts/storage-modes.md).

## Web, against a running desktop app

Source **Remote**, then endpoint, token, project root path, and branch. Easier: scan the QR code from the desktop app â€” see [Remote control](../guide/remote-control.md).

## What gets created

```text
design/            <- project folder
  active/          <- working folder, your cards
  actions/         <- action definitions
  history/         <- completed releases
  archived/        <- archived cards
md2.config.json    <- project configuration
```

Names are the defaults and all configurable. Everything is committed to your repository like any other file.

## Switching branch

Menu â†’ branch selector. The project reloads on the chosen branch, so cards follow the branch they were committed on.

9:* View and edit JSON files in a dedicated editor.
22:* Improved JSON editing, worktree operations, and feedback during project integration.
60:  * when in list view, this should be a new tab with a data editor
80:* In card view, add a `json-data` entry to `CardPopupService` and render the editor in the shared popup stack. In list view, extend `OpenFilesService`, `TabBar`, `TextEditorPane`, and project persistence with a JSON document kind so one tab exists per resolved project-relative path.
82:* Save valid JSON through the existing project persistence flow, using stable pretty-printed JSON and a final newline. Read-only projects render data but disable every mutation. If storage reports an external change while the document is dirty, keep the draft and warn instead of overwriting it.
84:* Render an array containing only objects as a table whose columns are the union of object field names in first-seen order. Render every other array, including empty and mixed-type arrays, with one `values` column. Missing object fields display an empty cell and remain missing until edited.
91:* Clicking a project-local `.json` link in card view opens one managed JSON popup anchored to the clicked link; clicking the same link again activates the existing popup.
92:* Clicking a project-local `.json` link in list view opens or activates one JSON tab for that resolved path.
94:* Objects display vertical fields. Object-only arrays display a table with the union of their field names. Primitive, mixed, and empty arrays display one `values` column. Root primitive values remain editable.
95:* Nested objects and arrays open through a drill-in control. Breadcrumb shows each traversed property or index and lets user return to any ancestor.
98:* Saving writes stable pretty-printed JSON through existing project persistence. Read-only projects cannot change data, and dirty drafts are not overwritten by external file changes.

entries.content:
## Findings

The feature has strong commercial value, but the website currently undersells it.

The release notes describe it only as “View and edit JSON files in a dedicated editor” ([release notes](</C:/Users/janbo/Documents/dev/md2/design/releases/0_12_0/release_notes.md:9>)). The actual feature is substantially richer:

- Open project-local JSON links directly from Markdown.
- Stay in context: a popup from card view or a persistent tab in list view.
- Edit objects as fields and object arrays as tables.
- Preserve JSON value types during inline editing.
- Navigate nested objects and arrays through breadcrumbs.
- Resize columns and use keyboard-accessible controls.
- Select multiple rows and add, delete, copy, cut, or paste records.
- Handle large arrays with virtualized, scroll-optimized rendering.
- Protect read-only projects and dirty drafts from unintended overwrites.

These capabilities are confirmed by the [core feature design](</C:/Users/janbo/Documents/dev/md2/design/releases/0.12.0/F_467_json_data_editor.md:80>), [object editor improvements](</C:/Users/janbo/Documents/dev/md2/design/releases/0.12.0/J_69_poor_object_editor_behaviour.md:37>), [array editor improvements](</C:/Users/janbo/Documents/dev/md2/design/releases/0.12.0/J_70_improve_json_list_editor.md:33>), and [large-list performance work](</C:/Users/janbo/Documents/dev/md2/design/releases/0.12.0/B_366_slow_json_list_editor.md:38>).

A good commercial positioning is:

> **Edit structured project data without dropping into raw JSON.**  
> Open a project-local JSON link from a card or design note. md² presents objects as fields and arrays as editable tables, with nested navigation, bulk row operations, and repository-backed saving—all without leaving the feature context.

This is more compelling than positioning it merely as another file editor. Its differentiator is the connection between project knowledge, structured datasets, and agent workflows.

## Best website placements

1. **GitHub README — highest commercial impact**

   Add a new section under “Why md²,” preferably immediately after “Local Markdown as shared project knowledge” and before “Run one action across structured data” in [README.md](</C:/Users/janbo/Documents/dev/md2/README.md:77>).

   Suggested heading: **Edit structured data in context**

   This is the main product landing page and the best place for the outcome-focused message, a screenshot or short video, and a link to the detailed guide. The [current public repository page](https://github.com/jan-bogaerts/md2) prominently explains diagrams, actions, and statistics, but not JSON editing.

2. **Dedicated JSON data editor guide**

   Create `docs/guide/json-data-editor.md`. This should be the canonical feature page covering:

   - how to create a project-local JSON link;
   - card-view popup versus list-view tab;
   - objects, arrays, primitives, and mixed arrays;
   - nested navigation and breadcrumbs;
   - row selection and bulk operations;
   - saving, read-only behavior, and external changes;
   - malformed JSON and other errors;
   - relevant limitations, including immutable property names.

   This page provides the destination for all commercial links without overloading the landing pages.

3. **Documentation homepage**

   Add the new guide to “Using md²” in [docs/README.md](</C:/Users/janbo/Documents/dev/md2/docs/README.md:40>) and expand the introduction with one concise sentence about editing linked structured data.

   The [deployed documentation homepage](https://jan-bogaerts.github.io/md2/) currently presents board, diagrams, stats, and list editing, but provides no path to discover this feature.

4. **List view guide**

   Update [docs/guide/text-view.md](</C:/Users/janbo/Documents/dev/md2/docs/guide/text-view.md:16>). It currently says tabs contain cards, Markdown files, or actions, which omits JSON documents. The [deployed List view page](https://jan-bogaerts.github.io/md2/guide/text-view.html) has the same gap.

   Add a focused “JSON data tabs” section describing structured layouts, nested navigation, editing operations, and tab reuse.

5. **Cards and files concept page**

   Expand “Files that are not cards” in [docs/concepts/cards-and-files.md](</C:/Users/janbo/Documents/dev/md2/docs/concepts/cards-and-files.md:94>). It currently discusses only other Markdown files.

   Explain that Markdown documents can link to project-local JSON data, and that those links open a structured editor rather than requiring an external editor. This reinforces the commercial story that repository files form connected project knowledge.

6. **For-each actions page**

# Edit JSON data

mdÂ² turns linked JSON into structured fields and tables, so you can inspect and update project data without switching to a raw JSON editor. Use it for inventories, test cases, migration inputs, agent datasets, and other structured files that belong with the work described in your Markdown.

## Open a JSON file

Add a Markdown link whose target ends in `.json`, then use the link's **Open** action:

```markdown
[API endpoints](../data/endpoints.json)
```

Relative paths resolve from the Markdown file containing the link. They are the best choice for files in the repository because the link keeps working across clones and worktrees.

Absolute Windows paths and `file:///` links can open JSON outside the active project. Those links are machine-specific and should not be used for shared project documentation.

Where the editor opens depends on the current workspace:

- In **Board** view, the JSON file opens in a resizable popup anchored to the link.
- In **List** view, the JSON file opens in a tab. Opening it again activates the existing tab instead of creating a duplicate.

The file must contain valid JSON. If it is missing, unreadable, or malformed, mdÂ² shows an error and does not open an editable document.

## Edit values

The editor chooses a layout from the value at the current JSON location:

| JSON value | Editor layout |
| --- | --- |
| Object | Resizable **Field** and **Value** columns. Property names remain fixed; scalar values are editable. |
| Array of objects | Table whose columns are the union of the objects' field names. |
| Empty, primitive, or mixed array | Table with one **values** column. |
| String, number, boolean, or `null` | A type-preserving scalar control. |

Editing a scalar keeps its JSON type. Number input is validated before it changes the document. A missing field in an object-array row is created when you edit its empty cell.

Drag a column separator to resize a table or use its keyboard controls. Wide arrays scroll horizontally. Large arrays use lightweight rows while you scroll and restore their editable controls when scrolling settles.

## Navigate nested data

Objects and arrays inside a field appear as **Open** controls. Open one to make it the current value. The breadcrumb above the editor shows the path from the file root and lets you return to any ancestor.

Array row numbers in the breadcrumb use zero-based JSON indexes, for example `[0]` for the first row.

## Work with array rows

Select one or more rows, then use the footer actions:

| Action | Behavior |
| --- | --- |
| **Add** | Appends an empty object to an object table, or `null` to other arrays. |
| **Delete** | Removes the selected rows. |
| **Copy** | Copies the selected values, in row order, as a JSON array. |
| **Cut** | Copies the selected rows and removes them after the clipboard write succeeds. |
| **Paste** | Inserts a JSON array after the last selected row, or at the end when no row is selected. |

Clipboard content for **Paste** must be a valid JSON array. Invalid content leaves the document unchanged and produces an error.

## Save and external changes

JSON inside the active project follows the normal project save and commit flow. JSON opened through an absolute local path is saved directly to that file instead.

When the project is read-only, you can browse the data but cannot change it. If a project JSON file changes outside mdÂ² while you have unsaved edits, mdÂ² keeps your draft and warns you instead of overwriting it.

## Use the data in an agent action

After preparing a JSON dataset, attach it to an agent action with **For each** to run the same focused prompt for every record. The attachment is saved with the draft or conversation; it is not a live link to the source file. See [Run an action for each JSON record](../actions/for-each.md).

See also: [List view](text-view.md), [Cards and files](../concepts/cards-and-files.md), [Git and commits](git-and-commits.md).
